Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.19596v1 [cs.SE] 14 Oct 2026 JevCoder: When Does Decision Delegation Pay Off in Code Repair? Jiahao Zhang Yifan Zhang Yu Huang Affiliation: Vanderbilt University, Nashville, Tennessee, USA Email: {jiahao.zhang,yifan.zhang.2,yu.huang}@vanderbilt.edu Abstract A coding agent repeatedly makes decisions as it repairs code. These decisions shape repair trajectories and affect the token cost of successive model requests. We ask which repair decisions can be delegated to a low-cost probabilistic judge to reduce token use while maintaining repair quality. The judges answer questions with probabilities over predefined answers, without generating explanations. We evaluate judgment quality across repair stages and test how individual interventions change subsequent repair work. We compare these interventions with unguided repair, which uses no judge, and with the same workflow using the repair model itself as the judge. The benefit depends on the work an intervention changes, rather than the cost of the judgment alone. Based on these studies, we propose JevCoder, a workflow built around Jev, a low-cost probabilistic judge. It combines code-snippet recommendations with action-type guidance and uses judgments to determine when to submit. We evaluate three repair models, each on the same 400 tasks: 200 from SWE-bench Verified and 200 from SWE-Bench Pro Verified. Compared to unguided repair, JevCoder reduces mean repair-model token use by 21.6%–50.6%, with higher observed repair rates across all three models. 1 Introduction Figure 1: In a simplified recorded SWE-Bench Pro Verified case, JevCoder uses Jev’s relevance probabilities to rank candidate snippets and supply selected code as the coding agent’s initial context. Figure 2: JevCoder delegates judgments to a shared probabilistic judge: Jev. Before repair, a program retrieves candidate code for the issue, Jev scores each snippet’s relevance, and the highest-scoring snippets enter the repair model’s initial context. After each command, program rules select relevant state questions for Jev and use its answers to suggest an action type. The repair model chooses the specific command. The stopping policy depends on the model class. For the larger API models (DeepSeek, Gemini), a Choice question on the latest check output (Pass: a previously failing check now passes; Rest: other outcomes) triggers direct submission. For the smaller model (Qwen), repeated No answers to whether the next step adds information trigger a reminder and then submission. A coding agent’s repair model chooses where to look, what to try, and when to stop. These choices affect how many steps the agent takes. When workflows resend interaction history, each request processes the accumulated context. Workflow design substantially affects this inference cost ( Xia et al., 2025 ; Ehrlich et al., 2025 ) . Assigning selected judgments to a cheaper model could reduce this expense. Whether delegation pays off depends on whether repair quality is maintained and on how it changes subsequent repair work. Coding agents receive feedback during repair or use verifiers to select candidate patches ( Pan et al., 2025 ; Jain et al., 2025 ) . SWE-PRM finds limited benefits from same-model supervision, but consistent gains with a stronger supervisor. In one setting, supervisor calls cost over six times as much as repair-model calls ( Gandhi et al., 2025 ) . We therefore ask which repair decisions are worth delegating to a low-cost judge. We study judges that return probabilities over predefined answers without generating explanations. Jev, TypeSafe’s decision model, provides structured answers and probabilities ( TypeSafe, 2026 ) . For binary questions, Jev returns the probability of “yes”. Choice returns probabilities for predefined options. Score uses a predefined rating scale, with a probability assigned to each level. Our experiments evaluate all three forms. JevCoder uses binary and Choice judgments to rank snippets or trigger repair interventions. We also use the repair model itself as a judge, reading probabilities for predefined answer tokens. Program rules determine when to ask a question and how to use the answer. Figure 1 illustrates this process for snippet recommendations. For the URL truncation issue, Jev assigns relevance 0.94 to the snippet that reads only the first child of an emphasis node. We assess judgment quality across repair stages and examine how individual interventions change subsequent repair work. Single-component experiments compare repair outcomes and resource use with unguided repair and, where available, same-model judging. They show that more accurate file rankings do not necessarily improve repair outcomes, and that retaining recommended snippets can reduce repair-model token use despite increasing context length. Building on these component results, we propose JevCoder for cost-efficient code repair (Figure 2 ). It uses code-snippet recommendations to guide initial code exploration and provides action-type guidance during repair. Its stopping policies use judgments of successful checks or repeated lack of progress to determine when the agent should end a repair attempt and submit its current patch. For each of three repair models, we compare JevCoder with unguided repair on the same 400 tasks: 200 from SWE-bench Verified and 200 from SWE-Bench Pro Verified. JevCoder reduces mean repair-model token use by 21.6%–50.6% and achieves higher observed repair rates for all three models. Compared with same-model judging, which helps distinguish workflow benefits from judging overhead, JevCoder uses 9.1% fewer tokens with DeepSeek and 23.3% fewer with Qwen. Code and evaluation results are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/jevcoder-artifact-8E62 . 2 Related Work Judgment in coding agents. Coding agents use feedback during repair and verifiers to select completed patches. SWE-PRM reads the issue and recent trajectory to diagnose errors, then returns natural-language feedback for the repair model’s next steps ( Gandhi et al., 2025 ) . Trained small critics can also provide this guidance ( Gandhi et al., 2026 ) . For completed candidates, SWE-Gym trains a verifier on successful and failed repair trajectories. Given the issue, a completed trajectory and its diff, the verifier uses answer probabilities to score candidate repairs ( Pan et al., 2025 ) . Testing adds execution evidence: reproduction tests for the issue and regression tests for existing behavior ( Xia et al., 2025 ) . Hybrid verification combines this evidence with learned scores to select a candidate ( Jain et al., 2025 ) . Replacing per-step model decisions with cheaper mechanisms is also studied outside repair: AutoTool predicts the next tool from transition statistics of past trajectories with minimal model inference ( Jia and Li, 2026 ) , and query routing sends requests to cheaper models when they suffice ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Ong et al., 2025 ) . JevCoder uses answer probabilities from fixed questions to trigger predefined interventions, which we evaluate across repair stages. LLM judgment and probability reliability. LLM judges evaluate responses through scores or pairwise comparisons ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) . Scores can be computed from probabilities assigned to rating tokens or predefined answers ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Pan et al., 2025 ) . In instruction-tuned models, the answer token with the highest probability can differ from the answer expressed in generated text ( Wang et al., 2024 ) . For software repair, SWE-RM separately evaluates how well scores distinguish successful from failed repairs and how closely predicted probabilities match observed success rates ( Shum et al., 2026 ) . We test judgment quality on specific repair questions and how using these judgments affects repair outcomes and resource use. 3 Study Setting Tasks and comparisons. We evaluate decision delegation on repository-level issue repair using a fixed sample of 200 tasks from SWE-bench Verified ( Chowdhury et al., 2024 ) and 200 from SWE-Bench Pro Verified ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) . Our sample covers Python, Go, JavaScript, and TypeScript repositories. The repair models are DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash ( DeepSeek-AI, 2026 ) , Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 ( Qwen Team, 2026b ) , and Gemini 3.8 Flash ( Google DeepMind, 2026 ) . For each model, full-workflow evaluation compares JevCoder with unguided repair on the same 400 tasks. For DeepSeek and Qwen, we also replace Jev with a same-model judge. Gemini’s API does not expose the answer-token probabilities required for this comparison. DeepSeek’s component studies use balanced samples of 72 SWE-bench Verified tasks and 118 SWE-Bench Pro Verified tasks, comprising all failures from the original unguided runs and an equal number of randomly sampled successes. Including both groups lets us measure repair gains and losses. Qwen component experiments follow similar procedures with model-specific samples; Gemini analyses focus on selected judgments in existing repair trajectories (Appendix C.2 ). The patch-outcome study uses 1,192 submitted-patch records from 343 tasks in SWE-bench Verified and SWE-Bench Pro v2 ( Deng et al., 2026 ) . Judges and evidence. Jev and the same-model judge receive the same question and evidence. We read the same-model judge’s probabilities for predefined answer tokens. Judgment-quality experiments also include the small LLM Qwen3.5-2B ( Qwen Team, 2026a ) . Evidence includes, for example, source snippets for relevance and command history for repetition. Reference patches and official test outcomes supply evaluation labels. The evidence supplied to each judge and its probability readouts are described in Appendices A , B , and C . Repair and resource measures. Repair rate is official pass@1: the fraction of tasks whose delivered patch passes the benchmark tests. Repair-model tokens count the repair model’s total input and output usage. Judge tokens are added for the same-model judging condition. Runtime estimates combine repair-model and tool-execution time with judge inference time. Remote API timings are adjusted by subtracting measured fixed connection delays; judge time is reported separately and included in the full-task total. Estimation and accounting details appear in Appendices C.3 and B . Each attempt is limited to 250 repair-model requests, a 3,000-second time limit, and US$3 in API costs. The first limit reached stops execution. Analysis. Differences are paired by task, with task-level percentile bootstrap 95% intervals. Primary summaries are mean token use and the median of paired runtime differences. Means summarize aggregate token use; runtime medians describe a typical task-level change. SWE-Bench Pro Verified opening comparisons are reweighted to the baseline failure and success proportions in the original 200 tasks. The 72-task estimates are unweighted. Raw repair counts refer to the tested sample. Each comparison uses one run per task and condition. The repair-loss criterion requires the lower bound of the paired 95% interval for the repair-rate difference to be at least − 10 -10 percentage points. Appendix D.4 provides sampling and analysis details, including the weights. 4 Judgment Quality We first examine which judgments Jev can make reliably at each stage of repair. The results guide the intervention studies in Section 5 and the design of JevCoder in Section 6 . A judge can support this choice by identifying useful starting points for the agent’s investigation. We first examine this ability at file level, using files modified by the reference patch as evaluation labels. We compare Jev with Qwen3.5-2B ( Qwen Team, 2026a ) , a small language model with similarly low inference overhead. A program retrieves 100 candidate files by combining BM25 retrieval with path and symbol matching. Both judges answer the same binary relevance question for each file, which we rank by the probability of a YES answer. On 162 SWE-Bench Pro Verified tasks, the top-ranked file is modified by the reference patch in 75.9% of tasks for Jev and 29.0% for Qwen3.5-2B. Median judgment time is below 0.15 seconds per file for both judges (Appendix C.3 ). File rankings identify where to look. We then assess relevance at a finer granularity to select individual code snippets for the agent’s initial context. Selection recall is measured against the source lines that the reference patch removes or replaces; 189 of the 200 SWE-Bench Pro Verified tasks have such lines. Jev’s selected snippets retain 81.6% of the reference lines covered by the candidates, compared with 78.0% for DeepSeek given the same candidates and questions (Appendix C.1 ). 4.2 Repair State and Next-Action Judgments What to try next depends on the stage reached during repair. For action-type guidance, we ask whether the agent has opened code relevant to the issue (code located) and whether a test or probe shows the reported failure (issue reproduced). We also assess whether recent actions repeat without new information (stalled repair) and whether a check after the latest edit shows the expected behavior (post-edit check). We derive evaluation labels from reference patches and recorded execution outcomes. We label code location using successful reads of reference-patch files, and reproduction using failed target tests or failed probes with exceptions. For stalled repair, we use command repetition without file writes; for post-edit checks, we use target checks passing since the latest edit. Full labeling rules appear in Appendix C . Each judge’s probability of a positive answer is the ranking score. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) measures how often positive states score above negative states, with ties counting as one half (0.5 indicates random ranking). Given the same questions and evidence, Jev achieves higher pooled AUROC than same-model judging for all four state questions across DeepSeek and Qwen trajectories (Table 1 ). We find the clearest discrimination for stalled repair (AUROC 0.968), compared with 0.738 for code location. We also test recognition of repeated commands. On 883 command pairs derived from recorded repair trajectories, Jev achieves 99.4% recall with a 0.6% false-positive rate at a probability threshold of 0.7. At the same threshold, Qwen3.5-2B achieves 95.5% recall with a 17.6% false-positive rate (Appendix C.1 ). Because the positives are rewritten rather than identical commands, this test covers repetition that an exact-match rule cannot detect. Before execution, the relevant question is whether a proposed command adds information or advances repair beyond recent commands and outputs. We compare judges through replay on 14,170 common command states, calibrating each threshold to block at most 1% of non-repeated commands that write source files. Under this constraint, the replayed policy blocks 61.9% of the scored steps in runs containing at least ten consecutive identical commands using Jev’s probabilities, compared with 28.0% using Qwen3.5-2B’s. We compare predicted probabilities of passing official tests with official repair outcomes on the patch sample described in Section 3 . Across four input configurations, Jev shows limited discrimination, with an AUROC of 0.562–0.595, compared with 0.638–0.684 for DeepSeek (Appendix C.1 ). A finer answer format could recover part of the gap. Jev’s Score interface returns probabilities over ordered levels of test success. On 840 common DeepSeek patch records, we use the probability of all target tests passing as the ranking score. Jev achieves an AUROC of 0.642, up from 0.581 for its binary question on the same records and close to that of DeepSeek scoring. The ordered question improves discrimination, but Jev still struggles to predict whether a patch will pass the official tests. We therefore examine whether Jev can recognize that a previously failing check now passes. On 52 matched states from DeepSeek trajectories, Jev distinguishes these transitions with an AUROC of 0.990, compared with 0.974 for DeepSeek judging (Table 1 ; Appendix C.2 ). Jev is near-perfect when the answer is recorded in the history and weak when it must be inferred. 5 Decision Delegation Across Repair Stages Judgment quality alone does not show whether delegation reduces the work needed for repair. We therefore evaluate each intervention separately against unguided repair, following repair from initial code exploration to submission. Each comparison links the change in repair work to token use and repair outcomes. Complete component comparisons and the evidence for selecting these components appear in Appendix D . 5.1 Code-Snippet Recommendations Useful code recommendations should reduce the repository exploration needed for repair. We first rank 100 candidate files by Jev’s relevance probabilities and supply retrieved source regions from the five highest-ranked files. With DeepSeek as the repair model, file recommendations use 5.8 fewer repair-model requests and 0.354M fewer repair-model tokens per task on average, while resolving a similar number of issues. File recommendations using Jev’s Score interface also reduce token use, but do not meet the prespecified repair-loss criterion (Table 2 ). Once the right files are open, the remaining decisions concern what to change inside them, which a file ranking does not inform (Appendix D.1 ). We therefore evaluate recommendations that select individual code snippets from retrieved source regions using Jev’s relevance probabilities. On the same sample, snippet recommendations resolve 68 issues, compared with 64 for file recommendations and 63 without recommendations. Relative to unguided repair, the weighted repair rate is 3.9 percentage points higher. Snippet recommendations also use 0.206M fewer repair-model tokens per task on average, with comparable runtime (Appendix D.1 ). Recommended snippets stay in the interaction history, so every later request carries their tokens. We therefore examine whether they reduce subsequent investigation by more than they add. Snippet recommendations also reduce read and search commands before the first editing command by 5.0 per task on average, with 0.126M fewer repair-model tokens over this period. On 116 matched DeepSeek tasks, removing the recommended snippets after ten repair-model requests increases mean repair-model token use by 0.538M per task (95% CI: 0.188M–0.930M), compared with retaining them throughout repair, and increases the paired median runtime by 32.1 seconds. Withdrawing the snippets increases subsequent investigation, so keeping them available reduces overall token use. On the 118-task Qwen comparison, mean repair-model token use is 0.230M lower per task with no loss in repair rate (Appendix D.1 ). 5.2 Action-Type Guidance Initial code provides a starting point, but the next useful action depends on what the agent learns during repair. Command blocking prevents execution of a command judged unlikely to add information and asks the model to propose an alternative. On Qwen, the lower bound of the repair-rate interval for this intervention falls below − 10 -10 percentage points (Table 2 ; Appendix D.2 ). Jev returns only a probability, so blocking can reject a command but cannot say what to do instead. After a tool result, Jev judges the current repair state, and a program maps its answers to action-type suggestions, such as reproducing the issue or editing code. The repair model chooses the specific command. With DeepSeek, Jev guidance resolves 45 issues, compared with 39 for unguided repair and 44 for same-model judging. Relative to unguided repair, the repair rate is 8.3 percentage points higher, and it uses 0.169M fewer repair-model tokens per task on average. Same-model judging adds 18.4 seconds to the paired median runtime relative to unguided repair; relative to same-model judging, Jev guidance shortens it by 26.1 seconds (Appendix D.2 ). 5.3 Submission and Early Stopping We next examine whether timely submission can avoid unnecessary repair-model requests. A previously failing test or reproduction check that now passes signals that repair may be complete. The agent must still decide to stop and submit. In unguided runs, Jev’s successful-check criterion is met in 130 of 400 DeepSeek runs, 57 of 400 Qwen runs, and 156 of 400 Gemini runs. After the first such check, the repair model still makes a median of nine, five, and 14 further requests, respectively. When Jev’s successful-check judgment meets the submission rule, the program can remind the repair model to submit or submit directly. With DeepSeek as the repair model, half of Jev’s 32 reminders are followed by submission within five subsequent repair-model requests. The program automatically submits the current patch after a qualifying judgment, ending repair without another repair-model request. The workflow resolves 45 issues, compared with 39 for unguided repair, and uses 0.295M fewer repair-model tokens per task on average (Appendix D.3 ). Stalled attempts without a successful-check signal need another basis for stopping. We test no-progress submission with Qwen3.8-27B, the smaller model in our study, whose runs more often stall before reaching a passing check. We ask the same question used for command blocking, but use consecutive low probabilities as a signal to end repair. Repeated no-progress judgments first trigger a reminder, and continued lack of progress leads the program to submit the current patch before executing the proposed command. No-progress submission and unguided repair each resolve 27 of the 72 SWE-Bench Pro Verified tasks (Appendix D.3 ). However, it reduces mean repair-model token use by 1.258M per task (95% CI: 0.905M–1.633M) and paired median runtime by 655.8 seconds (95% CI: 79.1–1,866.4). 6 JevCoder JevCoder combines the selected components into a complete repair workflow (Figure 2 ). Jev supplies probabilities for fixed questions, and program rules use them to decide how to intervene. Program rules handle decisions that can be determined directly from the trajectory. Jev interprets the evidence needed for the remaining judgments. The repair model generates code and chooses the commands to execute. Jev receives question-specific evidence from the repository and repair trajectory. All three repair models use snippet recommendations and action-type guidance. The stopping policy depends on the class of repair model: the two larger API models, DeepSeek and Gemini, stop on an observed successful check, and the smaller open-weight model, Qwen3.8-27B, stops on repeated lack of progress. Code-snippet recommendations. Before repair begins, a program retrieves source code using the issue and extracts candidate snippets from the retrieved source regions. Jev estimates whether each snippet is relevant to the issue. The program selects snippets in descending probability order within a length budget, merging overlapping source ranges. Selected snippets retain their file paths and line ranges, so the repair model can inspect the surrounding code. They are supplied before the first repair-model request and remain in the interaction history throughout repair. Action-type guidance. After each command, the program selects state questions based on the repair trajectory. It uses probability thresholds to map Jev’s answers to suggested action types. For example, when repair stalls before an edit, the program suggests editing if relevant code has been located and the issue reproduced. If the code is located but the issue has not been reproduced, it suggests probing instead. The program detects exact command repetition. Jev can identify commands that repeat searches or reads without obtaining new information, even when their wording differs. When consecutive judgments indicate stalled repair or a need to switch action types, the program sends a short note; the repair model chooses the command. We now examine whether combining them in JevCoder reduces the resources needed to resolve issues while maintaining repair quality. Table 3 compares the full JevCoder workflow with unguided repair. Same-model judging with DeepSeek and Qwen helps distinguish workflow benefits from judging overhead. Resource use and repair quality. JevCoder reduces mean repair-model token use by 21.6%–50.6% across all three models. Qwen shows the largest relative saving, with a statistically significant 50.6% reduction. JevCoder saves 0.756M repair-model tokens per task on average with Qwen (95% paired bootstrap CI: 0.590M–0.931M). The 95% intervals for DeepSeek and Gemini’s mean reductions also exclude zero (Appendix E ). JevCoder uses fewer tokens and achieves higher observed repair rates. All three JevCoder comparisons meet the prespecified repair-loss criterion. JevCoder newly resolves more tasks than it loses for every model and keeps 95.4% of DeepSeek’s and 94.9% of Gemini’s baseline-resolved tasks (Appendix E ). Runtime includes tool execution and judge inference. JevCoder reduces paired median runtime by 149.3 seconds for Qwen, 123.2 seconds for Gemini, and 9.5 seconds for DeepSeek; all three intervals exclude zero (Appendix E ). Same-model judging. Same-model judging tests whether the workflow can reduce token use when the repair model answers the same fixed questions. Relative to unguided repair, these conditions reduce mean repair-model tokens by 13.7% for DeepSeek and 35.5% for Qwen. Although both models use fewer tokens for repair requests than with JevCoder, adding the judging requests reverses this ordering. For Qwen, repair requests use 0.673M tokens per task, but judging adds 0.291M, bringing the total to 0.964M compared with JevCoder’s 0.739M. Same-model judging reduces the time spent on repair-model requests and tools, but its additional judging requests increase DeepSeek’s median runtime by 58.2%. For Qwen, median runtime falls by 15.2%, compared with 33.6% for JevCoder. Snippet ranking requires a separate request for each candidate, whereas Jev batches questions with shared evidence. JevCoder uses less judging time and shortens runtime for both models (Appendix E ). Jev usage is counted with its own tokenizer and reported separately: 0.152M, 0.193M, and 0.184M tokens per task with DeepSeek, Qwen, and Gemini; API costs including judge charges appear in Appendix E . Ablation study. To assess the components in combination, we remove one at a time from DeepSeek’s JevCoder workflow while keeping the others unchanged. Each removal lowers the observed repair rate and raises mean repair-model token use and paired median runtime. Removing snippet recommendations, for example, increases mean repair-model token use by 0.174M per task (Appendix E ). 8 Conclusion Our study identifies where decision delegation can reduce repair work and how to use the resulting judgments. Jev’s judgment-quality evaluations showed stronger discrimination for repair states than for patch outcomes. Recommended snippets shortened investigation before the first edit. Successful-check judgments enabled submission without further repair-model requests. Based on these findings, JevCoder combines code-snippet recommendations before repair, action-type guidance during repair, and a stopping policy adapted to model size. The larger API models stop on a successful check, while the smaller model stops on repeated lack of progress. JevCoder uses 21.6%–50.6% fewer repair-model tokens than unguided repair, with higher observed repair rates for all three models. Limitations We evaluate JevCoder with one version of Jev and three repair models on 400 tasks from SWE-bench Verified and SWE-Bench Pro Verified. All runs use the same agent framework. The models repair differently: the smaller model stalls more often, while the larger API models tend to continue repair long after their last edit. Each task and condition has one run, so we do not estimate run-to-run variance. The paired bootstrap intervals quantify uncertainty across tasks, and the mean token reductions exclude zero for all three models. File relevance and repair state labels are proxies. A file counts as relevant if the reference patch modifies it, and repair states are labeled by program rules rather than semantic correctness. We use these labels to compare judges and select interventions. Intervention benefits are evaluated using official pass@1 and repair-model token use. Runtime reflects serving conditions. Qwen runs on a local GPU service, while DeepSeek, Gemini, and Jev are remote APIs. For remote APIs, we subtract a measured fixed connection delay from the time recorded by the client. Within each comparison, the repair model uses the same serving setup for unguided repair and JevCoder. Tokens remain the primary resource measure. We use a fixed version of the commercial Jev service and record its usage separately from repair-model tokens. Saved answers allow the recorded judgments to be replayed without calling the service.
